intro: Khao Yai was Thailand's first national park, a sweep of monsoon forest and grassland on the hills north-east of Bangkok. Beside one of its forest trails stands a giant strangler fig whose trunk is a hollow cage of roots, the tree it once grew on long gone from the middle. A reader sent us its photograph, with daylight shining through the gaps in its roots.

trees.story:
"There used to be another tree in the middle," wrote the reader who sent us this fig from Khao Yai National Park, Thailand's first national park, and the photograph shows what they mean.

This is a strangler fig. These figs start life as a seed left by a bird high in the branches of another tree, and send their roots down its trunk to the soil. Over the years the roots thicken, press together and close round the host, which dies inside them and rots away. What stands in the forest now is the fig's own cage of roots, a lattice of grey columns climbing out of the red earth into a crown far above, with daylight shining through the gaps where the other tree once stood.

The scale is in the picture too. A person standing at its foot reaches barely past the first flare of the roots, which spread down the slope in great flat ribs.

The reader puts it at 500 years old and its girth at thirty metres. Those figures are theirs, not a measurement we have seen, and a fig with no single trunk is hard to measure or to date. Which fig it is we would like a reader to tell us.

Stand back on the path and look up into the hollow where the host tree used to be.

question_context: A reader who walked a forest trail in Khao Yai National Park sent us this fig, with a note that says it all: there used to be another tree in the middle. It is a strangler fig, a tree that begins as a seed in the branches of another and sends its roots down to the ground. Those roots thicken and fuse around the host until it dies and rots away inside them, and what is left is the fig's own trunk, a cage of grey roots, hollow in the centre. In the reader's photograph daylight shines through the gaps where the host once stood, and the roots flare out across a slope of red earth in great flat ribs, dwarfing a person at the foot. The reader puts the fig at about 500 years old and its girth at thirty metres; those are their figures, not a measurement we have seen, and a fig without a single trunk is hard to date. Khao Yai was Thailand's first national park; it charges an entry fee, and some of its forest trails are walked with a ranger or guide, so ask at the visitor centre before you set out.
